findings.claim: The title-history check only sees the last MaxVersions (5) snapshots. A part whose title was edited more than 5 times loses every '(part i/N)' title from memory_versions. After that, a shorter re-save leaves it active, even though it really was a part. The old code archived the derived key whatever its title said.
evidence: save.go:30-31 sets MaxVersions = 5, and save.go:389 deletes memory_versions rows with version <= next-MaxVersions on each snapshot.
The SQL at save.go:167-168 matches only the current title or a title still in memory_versions.
I did not run it. By reading, a part edited at least 6 times to titles that don't end '(part i/...)' matches neither clause, so it stays active as an orphan.

findings.claim: The title test is loose. Any memory on the derived or moved key whose current or past title ends ' (part i/<anything>)' is archived, case-insensitively, and the second pattern '% (part i/%)' matches non-numeric denominators such as '(part 2/x)'. Acceptable but wider than the first clause; a GLOB such as '* (part 2/[0-9]*)' would restrict it to digits.
evidence: The pattern parameters carry no '_' or '%' from user data, so no LIKE escaping problem arises.
Read save.go:90-200 and 222-252 in the target worktree, plus the grep hits for memory_versions and MaxVersions.
Checked the glob clauses for the '~<digits>' suffix, length and substr, and that the key is passed 5 times for 5 placeholders in order.
Checked that the 'exists' subquery correlates on memories.id inside an UPDATE, which is valid in SQLite.
